title: Adjectives and adverbs
subtitle: in a friendly way / freely
summary: Make adverbs from awkward adjectives and choose between pairs such as free/freely, late/lately and high/highly.

lesson.heading: Adjectives that already end in -ly
lesson.text: Many adverbs of manner (saying how something is done) are an adjective + -ly: *sudden* - *suddenly*, *happy* - *happily*. But when the adjective already ends in -ly (cowardly, elderly, friendly, kindly, lively, lonely, lovely) we don't add -ly again. Instead we use a prepositional phrase with **fashion**, **manner** or **way**.

examples.text: He smiled at me **in a friendly way**.
She waved her hands around **in a lively fashion**.
He was accused of behaving **in a cowardly manner** in the battle.

lesson.heading: Participle adjectives ending in -ed
lesson.text: Most participle adjectives ending in -ed have no adverb form, so we use a prepositional phrase instead, or a preposition and a related noun if there is one.

examples.text: They rose to greet me **in a subdued manner**.
The storm was unexpected. / The weather turned **unexpectedly** stormy.

lesson.note: Others with an -ly form: agitatedly, allegedly, deservedly, determinedly, disappointedly, excitedly, hurriedly, pointedly, repeatedly, reportedly, reputedly, supposedly, worriedly.

lesson.heading: Two forms, one meaning
lesson.text: Some adverbs have a form with -ly and a form without it, and we can sometimes use either without changing the meaning - though the -ly form is grammatically correct and more formal. The -ly form must be used when the adverb comes immediately before the verb.

examples.wrong: She quick ran towards the door

examples.text: Spread some butter on the bread as **thinly** as possible.

lesson.note: Also: cheap(ly), clean(ly), clear(ly), fine(ly), loud(ly), slow(ly), thin(ly).

lesson.heading: Two forms, two meanings
lesson.text: With other adverbs the two forms mean quite different things, so they are not interchangeable. The form without -ly usually keeps the concrete, physical meaning, while the -ly form is often figurative.

examples.text: The rise in car crime in the area is **deeply** worrying.
examples.note: deeply = very; *deep* would mean 'a long way'

examples.text: Pierre Evene manufactured the glass for which the town became **justly** renowned.

lesson.heading: Pairs to keep apart (1)
rows: She gave her time **free**. (= for no money)
She gave her time **freely**. (= willingly)
I arrived **late** for the concert. (= not on time)
I haven't seen Amy **lately**. (= recently)
He wandered **deep** into the forest and got lost. (= a long way)
He felt **deeply** hurt by her criticisms. (= very) / They loved each other **deeply**. (= very much)
You don't have to change trains. You can go **direct**. (= without stopping)
I'll be with you **directly**. (= very soon) / He saw Hassan **directly** ahead. (= straight)
It sounded awful - one of the choir members was singing **flat**.
This time I **flatly** refused to lend him any money. (= definitely; completely)

lesson.heading: Pairs to keep apart (2)
rows: He kicked the ball **high** over the goal.
Everyone thinks **highly** of her teaching. (= they think it is very good)
'Is Emil here yet?' 'He's **just** arrived.' / She looks **just** like her mother.
You can be **justly** proud of your musical achievements. (= rightly; justifiably)
Which of these cheeses do you like **most**?
Her novels are now **mostly** out of print. (= most of them) / We **mostly** go on holiday to France. (= usually)
They cut **short** their holiday when Lina fell ill. (= went home early)
The speaker will be arriving **shortly** (= soon). Please take your seats.
The door was **wide** open so I just went straight in. (= completely)
You won't have any problems getting the book. It's **widely** available. (= in many places)

lesson.text: If an adjective resists -ly, reach for *in a ... way / manner / fashion*, or a preposition plus a related noun: *in amazement*, *with despair*, *in / with satisfaction*.

exercises.prompt: I warned him ___ of the dangers on the mountain, but he insisted on going on.
exercises.explanation: Repeated is one of the -ed participle adjectives that does have an -ly adverb form.

exercises.prompt: We don't go out much in the evening. We ___ watch television.
exercises.explanation: Mostly here means 'usually'; most without -ly would mean 'more than anything else'.
She waved to me in a friendly way / manner / fashion. Friendly already ends in -ly, so it has no adverb form.

exercises.prompt: 'Still no news from Paul,' she said ___.
exercises.explanation: Disappointed is one of the participle adjectives with a regular -ly adverb.

exercises.prompt: The class was out of control and he put his head in his hands ___, feeling that he could do nothing.
exercises.explanation: Despaired has no adverb form, so we use a preposition + a related noun: in / with despair.

exercises.prompt: It is ___ the smallest post office in the country, although no one knows for certain.
exercises.explanation: Reputedly (= it is said to be) is one of the -ed adjectives that takes -ly.

exercises.prompt: He ran the company ___ and rarely let anything annoy him.
exercises.explanation: There is no adverb 'relaxedly', so we use in a relaxed way / manner / fashion.

exercises.prompt: I'm not in my office at the moment, but if you leave your name and number I'll get back to you ___.
I used to have to change in Amsterdam to get to Moscow, but now I can fly ___.
exercises.explanation: Go / fly direct = without stopping on the way.

exercises.statement: The prime minister was loud applauded by her audience.
exercises.explanation: The prime minister was loudly applauded by her audience. When the adverb comes immediately before the verb, the -ly form is needed.

exercises.prompt: How do you turn each adjective into an adverb?
categories: Use in a ... way / manner / fashion

exercises.prompt: Correct the adverb in 'I called Elena and she slow turned to face me.'
exercises.answer: I called Elena and she slowly turned to face me.
exercises.explanation: Slow and slowly can both follow the verb, but immediately before the verb only the -ly form is possible.
